comments.author: @jasonthomas5140
comments.text: at about 27:07 something very important is brought up that i feel deserves more attention than almost anything else in the realm of educational content:  the roadmap.  the rate at which things evolve in tech has always been fast, as was mentioned earlier, but this trend seems to be even crazier now than ever before, to the point where i have a real concern that if it takes me even a few months to learn a skill, that knowledge might be mostly unnecessary by the time i've acquired it.  add to this the problem that there is so much noise out there - everyone has different technologies or tools that they seem to think are the key things to learn, and from the naive perspective of someone who is just motivated to learn but doesn't know how to differentiate what's most critical to know, this can fragment focus and cost you valuable time that would be best spent on other material.  what i wish i had now was a good conceptual roadmap to follow with some specific topics/tools to learn which would help guide someone new to AI through this quagmire.  sort of a shortest path to garnering a conceptual understanding along with some practical skills that focuses on cultivating a minimum viable skillset.  and in addition i'd like to hear the reasoning behind why each tool/technology being learned will have some longevity.  i understand the point that specific industry expertise is probably one of the most valuable things - but not everyone has that, so for someone like myself who has a broader less focused set of skills or for a younger person just about to enter the workforce, i believe the importance of a good guide/roadmap to self-study cannot be overstated.

I always find it funny how the open source folks forget their own history. Open source software was never engaged in from a purely altruistic stand point. The altruism was just a nice side effect. The idea that a company that has hundreds of billions of dollars to facilitate the training is going to give up the secrets on its best models is ludicrous. especially when even the best shot from deepseek and qwen are not as good as the closed source frontier labs. When was the last time you say an open source release from the mistral guys? 

Finally you do not need open source to establish trust thats a rediculous statement. You need trust worthy behavior. Which all the labs have been thus far. Also, so long as you need multiple 10k plus gpu's to train these models the idea of training models from scratch is a fanciful idea. IF they want open source to blossom you need to be able to get GPT-5 performance from training on GPU's that cost at most what a couple high end gaming gpu's cost. Wihtout that kind of step change in training requirements. The best you can look forward to is being provided pretrained base models that you customize via an online service.

comments.author: @MikkoTikkanen
comments.text:
Development is most definitely not dead. You still 100% need to understand how good code is structured, what is needed for things to work, how to best integrate into outside systems etc. if you want to work on real projects with AI tools. Otherwise it will reward hack the f*ck out of the tasks you give it to. So you need to supervise it and in order to do that efficiently you need to know how to code.

Good example would be making an actual video game - I'm quite close to said industry and there is 0% possibility that you can currently do an actual proper video game, not a tech- or one-shot demo of Flappy Bird, without knowing how to code. I'm even actively trying to push full-time game developers to do that but the tools just do not support the way you need to work properly, for exampl with Unity. And the real work on game development is endless amount of iteration, and in order to do that you NEED to know how to code video games AND have the correct workflow.

If you do not know how to code, you will quickly reward-hack yourself into a corner, neck deep in technical debt. In the future this will not be the case but we are nowhere near that yet, GPT-5 and Claude 4.5 still reward hack like crazy.

Edit: And do note that I am pro-AI person that works with AI every day, not a doomer-boomer.
